title: Monsoon Winds and American Cups: How India's Most Unusual Coffee Is Finally Getting Its Global Moment
excerpt: Monsooned Malabar — the centuries-old Indian coffee transformed by Arabian Sea winds — is arriving at Starbucks Reserve stores in the U.S. this year, marking a quiet milestone for Indian coffee on the world stage.
body:
India is a tea country. Everyone knows that. What most people don't know is that coffee arrived on the subcontinent more than 200 years before tea did — and that one of the world's most unusual coffee preparations, born from a shipping accident centuries ago, is now making its way to Starbucks counters in the United States.

## The Accident That Created a Classic

The story of Monsooned Malabar coffee begins in the cargo holds of wooden sailing ships. During the 17th and 18th centuries, Indian coffee beans shipped to Europe endured a six-month journey in the hulls of vessels crossing the Arabian Sea. The monsoon winds, the salt air, and the relentless humidity caused the green beans to swell, turn a pale yellowish colour, and lose their natural acidity. When European merchants brewed them, they discovered something unexpected: a remarkably smooth, full-bodied coffee with deep woody and chocolatey notes, entirely unlike the bright, acidic coffees from Africa and the Americas.

By the time modern shipping eliminated those conditions, European demand for this peculiar Indian coffee hadn't waned. Producers along India's Malabar Coast began deliberately replicating the process. Today, high-quality Arabica beans are spread in large, open-walled warehouses in Mangalore and exposed to the southwest monsoon winds from June through August. Over 12 to 24 weeks, the beans absorb moisture, swell to nearly double their size, and undergo the same chemical transformation that once happened accidentally at sea.

## From Specialty Roasters to Starbucks Reserve

Monsooned Malabar has long been a favourite among specialty coffee enthusiasts. Roasters across Europe and North America carry it for its distinctive character — low acidity, heavy body, notes of sandalwood, dark chocolate, and spices that read like a description of an Indian kitchen. But it has remained a niche product, known mainly to the coffee-obsessed.

That is about to change. Tata Starbucks CEO Laxmi Narasimhan — himself of Indian origin — recently announced that Starbucks Reserve whole-bean Monsooned Malabar from India will be available at Reserve stores in both India and the United States later this year. The announcement came alongside a broader vision for Starbucks in India: 1,000 stores by 2028, opening at a pace of one every three days, with expansion into Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities.

For Monsooned Malabar, the Starbucks imprimatur is transformative. It takes a product that most Americans have never heard of and places it in the most visible specialty coffee retail environment in the world.

## Why It Matters for the Diaspora

India's coffee culture has always occupied an awkward space in the diaspora experience. NRIs in the U.S. know filter coffee — the strong, decoction-based brew served in a davara tumbler that is as much a South Indian identity marker as dosa or sambar. But Indian coffee as an origin — as a place that produces world-class beans on par with Ethiopian or Colombian coffee — has never broken through to mainstream American consciousness.

Monsooned Malabar changes that narrative. It offers something no other coffee-producing country can claim: a preparation method that is uniquely Indian, rooted in the geography of the Malabar Coast and the meteorology of the Arabian Sea monsoon. It is, quite literally, a coffee made by the Indian weather.

For the millions of Indian Americans who have watched turmeric lattes, chai concentrates, and ghee bulletproof coffee become mainstream American wellness trends — often without much acknowledgement of their Indian origins — the arrival of Monsooned Malabar at Starbucks Reserve carries a different weight. This time, the Indian origin isn't just an ingredient footnote. It is the entire story.

## What's Next

India currently accounts for roughly 3 percent of global coffee production, far behind Brazil, Vietnam, and Colombia. But the country's specialty coffee sector is growing rapidly, with estates in Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu winning international cupping awards and attracting attention from importers who once overlooked Indian origins entirely.

The Starbucks partnership could accelerate that trajectory dramatically. If Monsooned Malabar captures even a fraction of the curiosity that Ethiopian Yirgacheffe or Jamaican Blue Mountain has enjoyed among American coffee drinkers, it would mark the beginning of India's emergence as a serious specialty coffee origin — not just a tea country with a coffee side hustle, but a producer of some of the world's most distinctive and historically rich beans.
